concept: Parkinson's disease frontier platforms: dopaminergic cell replacement, gene therapy, digital biomarkers and wearables, AI, the gut-brain axis with body-first versus brain-first subtypes, and precision medicine
summary: Source-anchored research for Parkinson's disease frontier platforms: dopaminergic cell replacement, gene therapy, digital biomarkers and wearables, AI, the gut-brain axis with body-first versus brain-first subtypes, and precision medicine. Run status: COMPLETED.

narrative.documentConcept: AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression
narrative.text: Systematic reviews of machine learning in Parkinson's disease report a translation gap: very few systems have been adopted for real-world use, external validation is uncommon and accuracy is lower on external test sets, and data leakage is associated with inflated accuracy. The reviews also report high headline accuracy alongside low-quality evidence and a high risk of bias in most assessed studies, and a preprint reports that subject-aware splitting lowers reported performance. A machine learning study of longitudinal clinical data reports projections of progression and a replication in an independent cohort. The reviews' proportions describe the samples assessed, not the whole literature.

narrative.documentConcept: Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD
narrative.text: Wearable sensors, smartwatches and smartphone apps are studied as digital measures of Parkinson's disease for early detection, longitudinal change and regulatory endpoints. A UK Biobank accelerometry analysis reports better test performance for prodromal disease than models based on genetics, lifestyle, blood biochemistry or prodromal symptoms, and the multicenter WATCH-PD observational study reports device-derived features that differed between early Parkinson's disease and age-matched controls. Reviews report that most included studies were cross-sectional and call for standardization. A systematic review reports that no real-world walking speed measure has been fully validated by the FDA, and that a stride velocity endpoint approved by the EMA concerns a different disease. Consensus experts name the lack of clear reference values as the main challenge for digital mobility outcomes.

narrative.documentConcept: Dopaminergic cell replacement: bemdaneprocel and iPSC-derived neurons
narrative.text: Cell replacement for Parkinson's disease transplants dopaminergic progenitor cells derived from embryonic or induced pluripotent stem cells. Recent early-phase, open-label trials of an embryonic stem cell product and an induced pluripotent stem cell product report safety findings plus exploratory motor and imaging changes, and their authors caution about small cohorts, the absence of a control group and placebo effects. In one trial the authors state that risks were primarily associated with the immunosuppression regimen. A randomized, sham surgery-controlled phase three trial of the embryonic stem cell product is registered as recruiting, and a sponsor announced a conditional, time-limited approval in Japan of an induced pluripotent stem cell product.

narrative.documentConcept: Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors
narrative.text: Gene therapy for Parkinson's disease uses adeno-associated viral vectors that carry genes such as GDNF, AADC, GAD and neurturin, and, in registered programmes, GBA1. The early-phase GDNF study reports safety findings and exploratory motor changes, and its authors state that a randomized controlled study is planned to confirm them. In a sham-controlled GAD trial the scores fell in both arms, with a greater fall in the gene therapy arm, while a sham-controlled neurturin trial was not superior to sham surgery. A randomized, sham-controlled GDNF study is registered, and a registry record for an intravenous GBA1 programme is withdrawn. A regulator announcement about AADC deficiency concerns a different indication.

narrative.documentConcept: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
narrative.text: The brain-first versus body-first model proposes that alpha-synuclein pathology in Parkinson's disease begins either in the brain or in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system, and the proposers hypothesize that isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder is a prodromal phenotype of the body-first type. In their own review the proposers report that molecular imaging studies were generally in agreement with the model whereas structural imaging studies showed conflicting findings, a commentary notes limits on generalizability, and an autopsy preprint reports gut-restricted positivity in only a few subjects. Meta-analyses report gut microbiome alterations in Parkinson's disease, the authors of one state that differences in microbiome structure are small, and a later meta-analysis states that causality cannot be established. Two randomized fecal microbiota transplantation trials report different primary-outcome results.

narrative.documentConcept: PD subtypes and precision medicine
narrative.text: Studies in different cohorts report that Parkinson's disease subtypes differ in progression, and authors link the failure of disease-modifying trials in part to heterogeneity. Published schemes include data-driven clusters and the SynNeurGe research classification, which combines pathological alpha-synuclein, neurodegeneration defined by neuroimaging and pathogenic gene variants. Authors report that replication of published subtype classifications is limited. A genetic consortium preprint reports many potentially trial-eligible carriers of GBA1 and LRRK2 variants. Sponsors state that the LRRK2 kinase inhibitor BIIB122 did not meet its endpoints in an early-stage study that included people with or without a pathogenic LRRK2 variant and that they will discontinue development in idiopathic disease, while a study in carriers continues. Reports differ on motor progression in seed amplification assay negative disease.
